## Inside Anthropic's Form S-1: $16.3B H1 Revenue, an $80.7B GAAP Loss, and $518B in Cloud Lock-In

Let's look at the raw numbers inside Anthropic's S-1 filing (anthropicpbc-sx1.htm) before we trace where the money goes. On the surface, Anthropic's top-line growth is the fastest enterprise software ramp in Silicon Valley history, driven by Claude Code and enterprise API adoption. Full-year revenue jumped 12x from roughly $381 million in FY 2024 to $4.6 billion in FY 2025. In the first six months of 2026 alone (H1 2026), revenue hit $16.286 billion, with Q2 2026 generating $11.555 billion in a single quarter.

Then you look down the income statement and contractual footnotes, and two massive realities jump off the page:

- The $80.748 Billion H1 2026 GAAP Net Loss: While Anthropic narrowed its H1 2026 core operating loss to $693 million and generated $3.929 billion in positive operating cash flow, its GAAP net loss for those six months was a jaw-dropping $80.748 billion. Why? Because $72.388 billion of that loss came from non-cash mark-to-market revaluations of convertible notes and derivative liabilities issued to hyperscaler backers like Amazon and Google as Anthropic's private valuation surged toward $965 billion.

- The $518 Billion Take-or-Pay Cloud Mortgage: As reported by The New York Times on Google's $40B Anthropic commitment , Google committed up to $40 billion ($10 billion immediate cash plus $30 billion milestone-contingent financing) on top of its earlier $3B+ stake, while Amazon expanded its $8 billion investment by up to another $25 billion (up to $33 billion total). In exchange, Anthropic signed non-cancellable multi-year cloud purchase commitments totaling $111.1B to $114.5B to Google Cloud through July 2033, $110B to AWS through April 2036, and $31.4B to $44.9B to Microsoft Azure through 2033. Including Broadcom TPU leases and GPU neoclouds, Anthropic is locked into roughly $450B to $518B+ of fixed infrastructure obligations over the next decade, with nearly 80% structured as rigid take-or-pay contracts.

- The 16% Cloud Marketplace Toll: In 2025, 47% of Anthropic's total revenue ($2.16 billion) flowed through AWS Bedrock and Google Cloud Vertex AI marketplaces. For every dollar an enterprise spends on Claude through Bedrock or Vertex AI, Amazon and Google skim roughly 16 cents off the top in distribution fees before Anthropic pays those exact same clouds billions more to rent the underlying Trainium2 and TPU silicon.

## Dario Amodei's Two Essays vs. The S-1 Balance Sheet: How Much Does a 'Country of Geniuses' Cost?

To understand why Anthropic signed $518 billion in non-cancellable cloud leases, you have to read Dario Amodei's two foundational essays side by side with the S-1 risk factors. In October 2024, Dario published Machines of Loving Grace: How AI Could Transform the World for the Better . In that essay, he coined the phrase "a country of geniuses in a datacenter" : millions of autonomous frontier model instances smarter than Nobel Prize winners, running at 10x to 100x human speed, compressing 50 to 100 years of biological research, cancer cures, neuroscience, and economic development into a single 5 to 10 year window.

Fifteen months later, in January 2026, Dario published the darker companion essay, The Adolescence of Technology: Confronting and Overcoming the Risks of Powerful AI . Opening with Carl Sagan's famous question from Contact ("How did you survive this technological adolescence without destroying yourself?"), Dario mapped out five existential danger zones: autonomous alignment failures ( "I'm sorry, Dave" ), biological and cyber weaponization ( "A surprising and terrible empowerment" ), authoritarian surveillance ( "The odious apparatus" ), and in Section 4, titled "Player piano" after Kurt Vonnegut's novel, the risk of extreme economic disruption and wealth concentration in a tiny handful of compute-owning entities.

Here is the central paradox exposed by the S-1 filing: in The Adolescence of Technology , Dario warns that AI could concentrate unprecedented economic power in a few giant corporations. Yet nine months later, Anthropic's S-1 proves that surviving the compute race to build that "country of geniuses" required signing over $518 billion in take-or-pay infrastructure contracts to Google, Amazon, Microsoft, NVIDIA, and Broadcom. Even with Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust ( Class T shares) and founder super-voting stock ( Class F controlling 50.1%), a Public Benefit Corporation that owes half a trillion dollars in non-cancellable cloud rent cannot simply pause the treadmill when Wall Street expects quarterly growth.
